Can I tell you something? Before I moved here, everybody in Chicago warned me about the same things. What they talked about was crime, football and beaches.
That is the mainstream picture, yes. But it is not the beaches that surprise people when they get here. It is the size of everything.
That is true. What surprised me most was the inequality. Two streets apart, and it feels like two different countries.
The way I see it, it is not only money. What people outside Brazil rarely see is the difference in access: to hospitals, to good schools, even to sport.
Even to sport? I thought sport was the one thing everybody here had.
Football, maybe. When I played basketball in Franca, it was the infrastructure that made the difference. The interior has the talent. What it often lacks is the courts, the coaches and the money.
That is a perspective I never hear in Chicago. Somebody should bring that to light.
Maybe somebody will. What I would like to know is the opposite. What is one thing about Chicago that people get completely wrong?
What people outside Brazil rarely see is the difference in access.

What I would tentatively argue is that the system needs reform.

I have reported from Brazil for nine years, and my editors in New York usually want the same two stories. What they ask for is the Amazon, or football. What I keep offering them is something much less exciting. It is a bus. Every Monday, at four in the morning, a bus leaves a small town in the interior and takes patients to a hospital four hours away. Most of the people on that bus are not sick in a dramatic way. They need a specialist, and the nearest one is in another city. It was that bus that taught me what inequality in access really means. It is not a headline. It is a timetable. The story finally ran last year, and it sparked more debate than anything I wrote about the Amazon. It is the small stories that explain the big ones.

Here is the one trick that changed how my students sound in interviews. Listen to two sentences. The coach taught me discipline. It was the coach who taught me discipline. Same facts. But the second one tells the listener what to remember. That is what a cleft sentence does. It takes one piece of information and puts a light on it. What most learners forget is the voice. The cleft only works if you stress the part in the light. It was the coach who taught me discipline. Without that stress, it just sounds long. My other piece of advice is to use them carefully. One or two in an answer sound confident. Ten in an answer sound like a speech that somebody wrote for you. When everything is emphasized, nothing is.
